title: Edit Distance
source: Classic DP-on-strings warm-up (Levenshtein distance); prerequisite for the two-mode edit-distance problem reported by Infosys SP/DSE candidates (r/infosys, 2026)
statement:
You are given two strings `S` and `T` of lowercase English letters.

In one operation you may do one of the following to `S`:
- **insert** any character at any position,
- **delete** any character,
- **replace** any character with a different character.

Print the minimum number of operations needed to turn `S` into `T`.
inputFormat:
The first line contains the string `S`.
The second line contains the string `T`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum number of operations.
constraints:
- `1 ≤ |S|, |T| ≤ 1000`
- Both strings contain only lowercase letters `a`-`z`.

samples.explanation: `horse → rorse` (replace h) `→ rose` (delete r) `→ ros` (delete e).
One optimal sequence: delete `t`, replace `i→e`, replace `n→x`, replace `n→c`, insert `u`.

hints: Compare the **last** characters of the two prefixes. If they are equal, nothing needs to happen to them.
Otherwise the last operation on these prefixes was an insert, a delete or a replace - each one shrinks one or both prefixes by a character.
`dp[i][j]` = edit distance between `S[:i]` and `T[:j]`. `dp[i][0] = i`, `dp[0][j] = j`; if `S[i-1] == T[j-1]` then `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`, else `1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1])`.
editorial:
### State
`dp[i][j]` = minimum operations to convert the prefix `S[:i]` into the prefix `T[:j]`.

### Transitions
- `S[i-1] == T[j-1]`: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`
- otherwise `dp[i][j] = 1 + min(`
  - `dp[i-1][j]` (delete `S[i-1]`),
  - `dp[i][j-1]` (insert `T[j-1]`),
  - `dp[i-1][j-1]` (replace)`)`

### Base cases
`dp[0][j] = j` (insert everything), `dp[i][0] = i` (delete everything).

### Order
Row by row, left to right. Only the previous row is needed → `O(|T|)` memory.

**Time** `O(|S|·|T|)` ≈ `10^6`.

### Python tip
Inside the double loop avoid calling `min()` with three arguments and avoid 2D indexing; local variables and plain comparisons are ~2× faster.

### Common mistakes
- Off-by-one between string index `i-1` and table index `i`.
- Forgetting the base row/column (they are not zero).
- Adding `1` even when characters match.
